No unlearning signature is present. In every layer from 12 to 26, solution tokens and prompt tokens have similar per-token norms (ratio 0.89–1.11) and similar alignment with their own mean (cosine 0.46–0.67, solution tokens slightly higher only in layers 12–14). Prompt and solution means also point in similar directions (cosine 0.67–0.78). Combined with the flat math/nonmath update ratios on prompts in all layers, there is no "push toward a fixed vector" anywhere. That closes the RMU-style line.

Every structural and activation search has now come back natural. What remains is the failure profile itself. The model reads the numbers and computes correctly, but chooses the wrong *relation*, as in "20 + 70" where the problem needs "6×20 + 2×70". A corruption of how relational words ("each", "per", "times", "half", "more") are processed would produce exactly this.

Teacher-forced reference solutions can test it. At operator positions, a model with that defect would put low probability on the correct operator and prefer the wrong one, especially "+" where "×" is needed. First I need to see how the screening texts are formatted, in particular whether the "<<…>>" calculator annotations were stripped, so I can locate operator tokens reliably.

The screening texts are prompt plus reference solution with the annotations stripped ("2 * 7 = 14", "1050 / 14 = 75"), so operators appear as ordinary tokens between numbers.

From pass 8 (top-20 predictions on 150 DEV reference solutions) I will look at every position where the reference writes an arithmetic operator (+, −, *, /, ×). The model is uncertain whether an operator or a unit word comes next, so I restrict its top-20 distribution to the operator tokens alone. This isolates the *relational* choice: given that an operation follows, does the model pick the right one?

I report, per correct operator, how often the model's preferred operator matches and which wrong operator it prefers instead. Systematic substitutions, such as "+" preferred where "*" is correct well beyond the reverse, would point to a corrupted relation-processing mechanism. High, symmetric operator accuracy would put the deficit upstream, in which quantities get combined.

Operator choice is not systematically corrupted. Given the reference context, the model's preferred operator is correct 81% of the time for "+", 89% for "−", 70% for "×" and 80% for "/". The errors are spread over all alternatives, for example "×" confused with "−" (20) and "/" (17), not "+" (9). That is ordinary uncertainty, not a broken relation word, so the deficit lies in which quantities and relations the model sets up.

Every localized search has now come back natural. The one family not yet tried properly is the abliteration approach used for refusal directions. There the effective direction is chosen by layer: a difference-in-means direction that emerges abruptly at one layer, not just any layer's contrast. D1 took layer 10 without checking where the math contrast appears. An unlearning- or sandbag-style vector added at a specific layer would show up as a sudden *turn* in the math-minus-nonmath mean direction (low cosine between consecutive layers) together with a jump in its size.

Using pass 2 (500 prompts, all layers), I will compute that contrast per layer, averaged over content tokens and separately at the last prompt token. I report its relative size and the cosine to the previous layer. A smooth evolution (high consecutive cosines, gradual growth) means no injected math vector. An abrupt turn plus jump at a particular layer would mark the layer and direction to test next.

The math-minus-nonmath contrast grows smoothly over most of the depth, with one exception: layer 7. There it nearly doubles, from 0.26 to 0.46 of the residual norm on content tokens and from 0.18 to 0.39 at the last prompt token. At the last prompt token its direction also turns more than at any other layer (cosine 0.45 to the previous layer). Beyond layer 10 the contrast is stable (0.6–0.7) and turns little.

The large overall size is expected, since math word problems and poems or explanations differ in content. But the abrupt step at L7 marks the layer where most of the math-specific signal is written. Either L7's attention or its MLP writes it, and an implanted "math vector" would sit there.

The MLP part can be checked within the rules by applying L7's weights only to summary vectors. I take the mean activation difference (math minus nonmath prompts, content tokens, pass 6), map it through down_proj, and fold it through the post-feedforward norm scale. Then I compare that write with the measured jump in the contrast (L6→L7), and do the same for neighbouring layers 5–10. I also measure how concentrated the write is in its top neurons.
- If L7's MLP write aligns with the jump and a handful of neurons carry most of it, those neurons are a concrete candidate to ablate.
- If the write is diffuse, or the jump comes mostly from attention, I note that and move on.
